analysis.one_liner: Returns Native American remains and sacred objects held by museums and agencies to tribes and bans trading them.
analysis.headline: Both chambers passed it by voice vote in late October 1990, and President George H.W. Bush signed it into law on November 16, 1990, as Public Law 101-601.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill bans buying, selling, or profiting from Native American human remains, burial and sacred objects taken without the owners' consent, with criminal penalties. It requires federal agencies and museums that hold such items to inventory them, figure out which tribe they belong to, and return them when a tribe or descendant asks. It also sets rules for items dug up on federal or tribal lands in the future: diggings need a permit and the tribe's consent or consultation, and discoveries must be reported to the affected tribe. Tribes and museums can get federal grants to cover the cost of the process.
analysis.who_benefits: Native American tribes, Native Hawaiian organizations, and lineal descendants of the deceased. They gain the right to reclaim ancestors' remains and sacred objects held by museums and federal agencies, a ban on the trade in those items, ownership of cultural items found on federal and tribal lands, and federal grants to help cover repatriation costs [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Native tribes, Hawaiian organizations, and descendants

how_it_helps.text: Museums and federal agencies holding Native American remains, burial objects, and sacred objects must inventory them, identify their cultural affiliation, notify the affected tribes, and return items when affiliation is established and a claim is made [S2][S3].
Buying, selling, using for profit, or transporting for sale Native American remains or cultural objects without a right of possession is prohibited, with criminal penalties [S2][S3].
Native American cultural items excavated or discovered on federal or tribal lands belong to lineal descendants or, if they cannot be found, to the tribe with the closest cultural affiliation [S3].

Excavation of such items on federal or tribal lands requires a permit plus tribal consultation or consent, and anyone who discovers items during an activity must stop, protect them, and notify the tribe [S2][S3].

The Interior Secretary may assess civil penalties against museums that fail to comply, and noncompliant museums can lose federal grants; grants are also available to help tribes and museums carry out the law [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Museums and federal agencies bear the cost of inventorying and returning collections, and lose items they have held, some for a century or more. Anthropologists and archaeologists lose access to collections for study, except during approved scientific studies. Dealers and collectors in Native American artifacts lose a legal trade in remains and sacred objects. Taxpayers fund the grants and the federal oversight committee [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The law allows museums to hold items until a specific scientific study is completed before returning them, and it still permits excavation of remains and objects under permits, with only consultation rather than consent required on federal lands [S2][S3].

Museums and agencies must fund inventories and documentation of large collections, and the process for establishing cultural affiliation can be slow and contested, which some in the museum and research community argued imposed significant costs and documentation burdens [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to tribes and descendants — the return of ancestors' remains and sacred objects and an end to a commercial trade in them — are substantial and largely one-sided, while the costs fall on museums and researchers in the form of inventories, returned collections, and delayed study. The main honest critique is that the process is slow and leaves museums holding items until studies finish, but the law passed with no recorded opposition vote in either chamber.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it by voice vote on October 22, the Senate passed it with two amendments by voice vote on October 26, the House agreed to the Senate amendments by unanimous consent the next day, and the President signed it on November 16, 1990, making it Public Law 101-601.

narrative.text: Rep. Morris Udall introduced the bill on July 10, 1990, and hearings were held in the Interior and Insular Affairs Committee within a week [S1][S5].
The committee received comments from the Army Corps of Engineers, the Justice Department, and the Interior Department before marking the bill up and reporting it amended on October 15, 1990 [S5].

The House passed the amended bill by voice vote on October 22, 1990, under a procedure (suspension of the rules) used for noncontroversial bills that skips amendments and requires a two-thirds majority [S5].
The Senate passed the bill with two amendments by voice vote on October 26, 1990, after briefly vitiating its earlier passage from October 25 to re-adopt the same amendments [S5].
The House agreed to the Senate amendments by unanimous consent on October 27, 1990, and the President signed the bill on November 16, 1990, making it Public Law 101-601 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Native American tribes, Native Hawaiian organizations, and descendants gained a legal right to reclaim ancestors' remains and sacred objects; museums, agencies, and the artifact trade bore the costs.

for.name: Rep. Morris K. Udall

for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, held hearings within a week of introduction, brought it through markup, and reported it amended to the House floor.

for.what_they_did: Moved to suspend the rules and pass the bill as amended, which the House adopted by voice vote.

for.what_they_did: Asked unanimous consent for the House to accept the Senate amendments, clearing the way for enactment.

for.name: Sen. Slade Gorton

sides.party_line_note: The bill passed both chambers by voice vote — the record shows no recorded opposition or party split — and a Republican president signed it.

industries.note: They must inventory, identify, and return remains and sacred objects, face civil penalties and grant ineligibility for noncompliance, but the law leaves them as the ongoing custodians and gatekeepers of most collections and pays federal grants for their inventory work.
Researchers lose open access to Native American remains and collections, which had long been used for study, though the law allows holding items to complete specific scientific studies.

industries.industry: Art and antiquities dealers and auction houses
industries.note: The law bans buying, selling, or profiting from Native American remains and sacred objects lacking a right of possession, with criminal penalties, ending a legal trade in these items.
